topic: Fine-tuning vs prompting: LoRA, PEFT, when not to
why: Fine-tuning is the most expensive wrong answer an FDE can give in a scoping call: it converts a two-week prompt-and-retrieval engagement into a six-month labelling programme, and the customer's ML-curious VP will usually ask for it by name in the first hour. Your job is to be the person who can say 'here is the measurement showing prompting already clears your bar, and here is the number that would change my mind' — which is only credible if you have actually shipped a LoRA run and can talk about masking, rank, and adapter serving without hand-waving. And when a tune genuinely is the right call — a rigid output format, a domain the tokenizer mangles, or a cost target only a small tuned model hits — you have to be able to build it, evaluate it against the baseline, and own the retraining tail you just sold.
prerequisites: Topic 46 (prompt engineering as code): a versioned prompt, a structured-output schema, and a regression set you can re-run with one command — the tune has to beat that exact artefact, not a vibe.

Topic 49 (RAG at depth): enough retrieval fluency to rule out 'the right chunk was never in context' before you propose changing weights, since most 'the model doesn't know our domain' complaints are retrieval bugs.

Topic 45 (LLM fundamentals): tokenizers and chat templates, the attention projections (q_proj/k_proj/v_proj/o_proj) and MLP blocks (gate/up/down_proj), and precision formats — fp32, bf16, fp16, int8, int4.

Working PyTorch-adjacent Python: `transformers`, `datasets`, a Colab or single-GPU runtime, `nvidia-smi`, and the ability to read a CUDA OOM traceback and know which of batch size, sequence length, or model size to cut.

Supervised ML evaluation basics: entity-level train/val/test splits, precision/recall/F1, confusion matrices, class imbalance, overfitting, and bootstrap confidence intervals — you cannot write the memo without them.

A real labelled dataset from a customer-like domain (200+ examples minimum, 1000+ preferred) and permission to use it; without labels this topic degenerates into a tutorial you cannot generalise from.

subtopics.name: The gate: three questions that decide fine-tune vs prompt
subtopics.learn: Internalise the decision gate so you can run it live in a scoping call. Fine-tuning reliably changes behaviour — output format adherence, tone, a task-specific decision boundary, and cost/latency by letting a smaller model do a narrow job. It does not reliably add knowledge: facts baked into weights are lossy, unverifiable, un-citable, and can only be updated by retraining, which is why retrieval owns that job. The three questions: is the failure a knowledge gap or a behaviour gap; can you get 500+ correct input/output pairs that match production traffic; and is there a measured baseline with a stated delta the tune must beat. Any 'no' means stop and say so out loud.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform docs - Fine-tuning guide

subtopics.name: Baseline discipline: the control you are required to beat
subtopics.learn: Before any training, freeze a baseline and make it reproducible by script: best prompted configuration (few-shot examples, output schema, retrieval on/off) scored on a held-out set of 100+ labelled customer examples, with per-class metrics, a confidence interval, measured p50/p95 latency, and cost per 1000 calls. Record the prompt hash, the model ID including snapshot, temperature, and the eval commit SHA. Learn that most 'the model isn't good enough' claims collapse here: a tighter JSON schema, eight nearest-neighbour-selected few-shot examples, or fixing chunk boundaries usually moves the number further than a LoRA will. If you cannot re-run the baseline with one command, you do not have a baseline and you are not allowed to fine-tune yet.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Metrics and scoring: quantifying the quality of predictions

subtopics.name: Full fine-tuning memory arithmetic, and why PEFT exists
subtopics.learn: Derive on paper why full fine-tuning is usually off the table. Per parameter you pay roughly 2 bytes (bf16 weights) + 2 (gradients) + 4+4 (Adam first and second moments in fp32) + 4 (fp32 master weights) which is about 16 bytes/param before activations — so a 7B model wants roughly 112 GB and an 8B roughly 128 GB, and activation memory on top scales with batch x seq_len x layers. Know the levers that soften but do not change the conclusion — gradient checkpointing trades about 30% extra compute for activation memory, gradient accumulation trades wall-clock for effective batch, ZeRO/FSDP shards across GPUs — and the one that does change it: freeze the base so gradients and optimizer states exist only for a tiny trainable subset.

resource.label: Hugging Face Transformers - GPU training methods and memory optimization

subtopics.name: LoRA mechanism: h = Wx + (alpha/r)·B(Ax)
subtopics.learn: Be able to derive LoRA on a whiteboard from memory. For a frozen weight W of shape (d, k) you learn a low-rank update dW = B·A with A of shape (r, k) initialised Gaussian and B of shape (d, r) initialised to zeros, so dW = 0 at step 0 and training starts exactly at the base model's behaviour. Forward is h = Wx + (alpha/r)·B(Ax); only A and B get gradients, so optimizer state is O(r·(d+k)) instead of O(d·k) — typically 0.1-1% of parameters trainable. Know the three consequences that matter commercially: the adapter is tens of megabytes, it can be merged so inference latency is unchanged, and one base model can host many adapters. Read the paper's ablations on which matrices to adapt and on how little rank is actually needed.

resource.label: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (arXiv 2106.09685)

subtopics.name: LoraConfig field by field, and what each one breaks
subtopics.learn: Know every field you will set and its failure mode. `r` (8-64 typical; higher rank means more capacity and more overfitting on small data). `lora_alpha` (the update is scaled by alpha/r, so alpha = 2r is a common convention and changing r without changing alpha silently changes the effective learning rate). `target_modules` — attention-only `["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj"]` versus adding the MLP `["gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj"]`, where MLP targeting is usually what buys format adherence, with `"all-linear"` as the lazy default. `lora_dropout`, `bias`, `task_type` (`CAUSAL_LM` vs `SEQ_CLS`; the wrong value quietly drops the head), and `modules_to_save` (required for a new classification head or resized embeddings, otherwise you save an adapter that cannot reproduce your own eval).

resource.label: Hugging Face PEFT - LoRA API reference (LoraConfig)

subtopics.name: PEFT wiring: wrap, verify, save, hot-swap
subtopics.learn: Get the mechanics into muscle memory: `get_peft_model(model, LoraConfig(...))` then immediately `print_trainable_parameters()` and sanity-check the ratio. If it reports 100% you have not frozen anything; if it reports 0.00% your `target_modules` matched nothing — that is the number one silent failure in this topic and it produces a perfectly plausible loss curve. Know that `save_pretrained()` writes only the adapter, `PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, adapter_dir)` reloads it, and `add_adapter`/`set_adapter`/the `disable_adapter()` context manager let you A/B base versus tuned behaviour inside a single process — which is the fastest way to produce the comparison your memo needs.

resource.label: Hugging Face PEFT - Quicktour

subtopics.name: QLoRA: 4-bit frozen base, 16-bit adapters
subtopics.learn: Understand exactly what QLoRA changes and what it costs. The frozen base is quantized to 4-bit NF4, a datatype chosen to be information-theoretically well matched to normally-distributed weights; LoRA adapters stay in bf16; blocks are dequantized on the fly during forward and backward. Add double quantization (quantizing the quantization constants, saving roughly 0.37 bits/param) and paged optimizers to survive the memory spikes that otherwise OOM mid-epoch. The trade you must be able to state: a 7B tune fits in roughly 10 GB and a 13B in roughly 16 GB, at roughly 30-50% slower steps, and the quantized base is a training-time device — serving precision is a separate decision you make later.

resource.label: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs (arXiv 2305.14314)

subtopics.name: Quantized training in practice, and its failure signatures
subtopics.learn: Configure it for real: `BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16, bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True)`, then `prepare_model_for_kbit_training()` to upcast layer norms, enable gradient checkpointing, and disable `use_cache`. Learn the signatures so you diagnose in minutes not hours: NaN loss from fp16 compute dtype with a high learning rate (prefer bf16 where the GPU supports it); loss flat at a constant because nothing is trainable; and a completed run whose adapter cannot be merged because the base was loaded in 4-bit and `merge_and_unload()` was called without reloading the base at full precision.

resource.label: Hugging Face PEFT - Quantization developer guide

subtopics.name: The rest of the PEFT family and when LoRA is the wrong pick
subtopics.learn: Know the alternatives well enough not to reach for LoRA reflexively. IA3 learns rescaling vectors on key, value and feed-forward activations with far fewer parameters than LoRA and is strong for few-shot classification. Prompt tuning, prefix tuning and P-tuning learn soft tokens prepended to the input — they consume context window, cannot be merged into weights, and are usually weaker at format control. DoRA decomposes the update into magnitude and direction and tends to beat LoRA at low rank for extra step time. And know the boundary: for single-label classification with clean labels, none of these should be your answer — a fine-tuned encoder wins on every axis you will be asked about.

resource.label: Hugging Face PEFT - IA3 reference

subtopics.name: Dataset construction: chat template, loss masking, EOS
subtopics.learn: This is where tunes actually fail, not in the optimizer. Use the model's own template via `tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False)` — a template mismatch between training and serving is the single most common cause of a tuned model that is worse than the base in production while looking fine offline. Mask the prompt so loss is computed only over completion tokens (TRL's completion-only collator / `completion_only_loss`), otherwise you are training the model to generate the user's turns. Verify EOS is appended and not masked to -100, or generations never terminate and run to `max_tokens`. Decode a batch after collation and read it with your own eyes before launching the run.

resource.label: Hugging Face Transformers - Chat templates

subtopics.name: Dataset formats and splitting without leakage
subtopics.learn: Know the two shapes TRL accepts — prompt/completion pairs and conversational `messages` lists — and that the template is applied automatically for conversational data but not for raw text, which is a quiet source of double-templating. Split by customer entity (document, account, ticket thread, author) rather than by row: near-duplicate rows straddling the split is why a tune reports +12 points offline and zero online. Deduplicate first with normalised-text hashing or MinHash. Decide packing versus padding deliberately — packing concatenates samples for throughput but bleeds one example into the next unless boundaries are respected. Hold the test set back and do not look at it until the memo.

resource.label: Hugging Face TRL - Dataset formats and types

subtopics.name: The SFT run: the SFTConfig knobs that actually matter
subtopics.learn: Configure `SFTTrainer`/`SFTConfig` with intent: `learning_rate` of 1e-4 to 2e-4 for LoRA (10-100x higher than full fine-tuning — carrying over a 2e-5 habit produces a run that barely moves), `num_train_epochs` of 1-3 (under 2k examples, three epochs is usually already overfitting), `per_device_train_batch_size` x `gradient_accumulation_steps` as your effective batch, `lr_scheduler_type="cosine"` with `warmup_ratio` around 0.03, `max_length` chosen from an actual token-length histogram because silent truncation deletes your labels, `bf16=True`, `gradient_checkpointing=True`, `eval_strategy="steps"`, and a fixed `seed`. Always smoke-test with 32 examples and `max_steps=5` before spending GPU budget.

resource.label: Hugging Face TRL - SFT Trainer

subtopics.name: Reading the run: overfitting, forgetting, PEFT-specific bugs
subtopics.learn: Watch train and eval loss together. Eval loss rising while train loss falls is overfitting — keep `load_best_model_at_end` with an explicit `metric_for_best_model` and ship the earlier checkpoint. Loss flat from step 0 means nothing is learning: check trainable parameters are non-zero, the learning rate is non-zero, and the labels are not all -100. Regression on tasks outside the tuning distribution is catastrophic forgetting; measure it deliberately with a general-capability holdout and mitigate with lower rank, fewer epochs, or mixing in 10-20% general data. Learn the PEFT-specific gotchas from the troubleshooting guide: unmatched target modules, adapter/base dtype mismatch, and a tokenizer not saved alongside the adapter.

resource.label: Hugging Face PEFT - Troubleshooting

subtopics.name: Evaluating the tune against the baseline honestly
subtopics.learn: Score baseline and tune with the same script on the same untouched test set, reporting the same things: task metric, per-class breakdown, confusion matrix, format-validity rate, refusal rate, p95 latency, and cost per 1000 calls. Attach uncertainty — at n=200 a three-point difference is inside the noise, so use a bootstrap CI or a paired test (McNemar for paired binary outcomes) before you claim a win. Explicitly look for what regressed rather than only what improved, including behaviour on out-of-distribution inputs. Write down, before you see the result, the delta that would justify the ongoing cost; deciding afterwards is how teams talk themselves into shipping noise.

resource.label: scikit-learn - Metrics and scoring

subtopics.name: The adapter artefact: what you are actually shipping
subtopics.learn: Open the output directory and know every file. `adapter_config.json` carries `base_model_name_or_path`, `r`, `lora_alpha`, `target_modules` and `peft_type` — this is your reproducibility record and it belongs in version control. `adapter_model.safetensors` holds the A and B matrices keyed by module path, typically tens of megabytes. Know that the adapter is meaningless without the exact base checkpoint, so pin the base by commit revision rather than a moving tag; that the tokenizer must be saved next to it; and that safetensors is preferred over `.bin` because loading a pickle from an untrusted source executes arbitrary code — which matters the moment adapters cross a customer boundary.

resource.label: Hugging Face PEFT - PEFT checkpoint format

subtopics.name: Serving: merged weights versus runtime adapters
subtopics.learn: Know both deployment shapes and their trade-offs cold. `merge_and_unload()` folds (alpha/r)·BA into W, giving zero added inference latency and an ordinary model artefact — at the cost of a full-size checkpoint per variant, no hot-swap, and precision loss if you merge into a quantized base. Alternatively serve adapters at runtime: vLLM with `--enable-lora`, `--max-loras`, `--max-lora-rank`, and a per-request `LoRARequest`, which lets a single GPU serve many per-tenant adapters at a modest throughput cost. Know what bites: `max_lora_rank` must be at least your `r`, the server must support the modules you targeted, and throughput degrades as distinct adapters per batch increases.

resource.label: vLLM docs - LoRA Adapters

subtopics.name: Managed fine-tuning on hosted APIs: what you trade away
subtopics.learn: Know the hosted path end to end: upload JSONL, pick a base, wait for a job, receive a tuned model ID, then pay a training fee plus usually a premium per-token inference rate and sometimes an hourly hosting charge for a provisioned custom model. Be precise about what you give up: you cannot inspect or export the adapter, you cannot move it to another provider or on-prem, the base can be deprecated out from under you and force a retrain, and the customer's training data leaves their boundary — which is frequently the entire reason a regulated buyer says no. Know when it still wins: no GPU operations, no serving to run, and a compliance story the vendor already owns.

resource.label: Amazon Bedrock User Guide - Customize your model

subtopics.name: The cheaper thing that usually wins the bake-off
subtopics.learn: Before recommending a generative fine-tune, cost the alternatives on the identical eval set. (a) A fine-tuned encoder classifier in the 100-400M parameter range trains in minutes and serves in single-digit milliseconds on CPU-class hardware. (b) Frozen embeddings plus logistic regression gives calibrated probabilities and a threshold you can tune to the customer's precision/recall trade-off — which is what an ops team actually wants. (c) SetFit reaches strong accuracy with 8-64 examples per class, which matters when labels are the constraint. (d) Distillation: use the frontier model to label 10k examples, then train the small one. For classification these routinely match a LoRA'd 7B at one to two orders of magnitude less inference cost — which is the memo you were asked to write.

resource.label: Hugging Face SetFit documentation

subtopics.name: Total cost of ownership and the retraining tail
subtopics.learn: Build the cost model the memo lives or dies on. One-off: labelling hours x loaded rate, GPU-hours x price, engineer-days for the pipeline and eval. Recurring: inference cost delta versus baseline x projected monthly volume, adapter hosting or provisioned throughput, and periodic eval runs. Then the tail nobody budgets: every base-model upgrade invalidates the adapter, every schema or policy change invalidates the training data, and drift forces a re-label plus retrain roughly quarterly. Compare that against the prompted baseline's cost curve, which improves for free every time a vendor ships a cheaper or better model. State a break-even monthly volume explicitly and put it in the memo as a number.

resource.label: Google Cloud - Introduction to tuning (Vertex AI generative AI)

subtopics.name: Governance: data rights, PII, licences, model cards
subtopics.learn: Settle these before a single byte of customer data becomes a gradient. Confirm the contract permits training on the data and states who owns the resulting weights. Strip or pseudonymise PII and know that memorisation is real, so an adapter trained on one tenant's data must never serve another tenant. Check the base model licence — Llama's community licence, Gemma's terms of use, and Apache-2.0 differ materially on redistribution, naming, and acceptable use, and merged weights are a derivative work. Then ship a model card: base model plus pinned revision, data provenance and date range, eval numbers with the test-set definition, known failure modes, and the trigger that forces retraining.

resource.label: Hugging Face Hub - Model Cards

outcomes: You can run the fine-tune-versus-prompt gate live in a scoping call and produce, within ten minutes, a written recommendation plus the specific measurement that would reverse it.

You can execute a QLoRA supervised fine-tune of a 7B-class model on a single free-tier GPU end to end — chat-template formatting, completion-only loss masking, SFTConfig, checkpoint selection — and reload the adapter in a fresh process to reproduce your eval scores exactly.

You can read a LoraConfig and state its trainable-parameter percentage, approximate memory footprint, and overfitting risk, and explain what changing r without changing lora_alpha does to the effective update.

You can produce a four-arm comparison table — prompted baseline, few-shot plus schema, LoRA, encoder classifier — on one untouched test set with task metric, confidence interval, p95 latency, and cost per 1000 calls.
You can detect catastrophic forgetting using an explicit off-distribution holdout, quantify it, and name the mitigation you chose and why you rejected the others.
You can deploy the same adapter both ways — merged into base weights and hot-loaded at runtime under vLLM — and state the throughput, latency, and operational trade-off for a multi-tenant customer.

You can write a one-page decision memo recommending against fine-tuning, with a break-even monthly volume and a named trigger for revisiting, and defend it to a stakeholder who arrived asking for a custom model.
You can list, unprompted, the contractual, PII, tenancy, and licence questions that must be answered before customer data is used for training.
failureModes: Training with a chat template that does not match the one the serving stack applies at inference, so the tuned model underperforms the base in production while the offline eval looks like a clean win.

Computing loss over prompt tokens as well as completions — producing a model that cheerfully generates the user's next turn — or masking out EOS so generations never terminate and every request runs to max_tokens.
Splitting the dataset by row when the customer's corpus is full of near-duplicate tickets and boilerplate documents, reporting a double-digit offline gain that evaporates entirely on live traffic.
`target_modules` silently matching nothing (or the wrong `task_type` dropping the head), so four GPU-hours and a plausible loss curve later you ship the unchanged base model under a new name.

Fine-tuning to inject facts — product catalogue, policy numbers, org chart — producing confident, uncitable, un-updatable errors that retrieval would have solved and that now require a full retrain to correct.
Shipping a per-customer adapter without pinning the base-model revision, then losing the ability to reproduce, re-merge, or re-serve the tuned behaviour after the base is upgraded or deprecated.
Serving a tenant-specific adapter trained on PII from a shared multi-tenant endpoint, creating a cross-tenant leakage path through memorisation that surfaces in the customer's first security review.
interviewQuestions: A customer's head of data opens with 'our domain is special, we need a model fine-tuned on our 40 million support tickets.' Run your discovery on the spot: what do you ask, what do you measure in week one, and what would have to be true for you to agree?

Derive LoRA at the whiteboard. Then tell me precisely what changes in the GPU memory profile versus full fine-tuning, why the alpha-over-r scaling term appears in the forward pass, and what happens to inference latency after merging.
Your LoRA'd model scores 91% on the held-out set against 86% for the prompted baseline, on 200 examples. The customer wants to ship on Friday. What do you say, and what do you do before Friday?
A tuned model that passed eval is performing worse than the base model in production. Give me your ordered debugging plan and say what evidence would move you from one hypothesis to the next.

Design the deployment for 40 enterprise tenants who each want the assistant tuned on their own style guide, under a fixed two-GPU budget. Where do adapters live, how does a request route to the right one, and what breaks first as tenants grow?
When would you put a 300M-parameter encoder in front of a customer instead of a fine-tuned 8B generative model, and how would you prove it to a buyer who has an LLM line item to spend?

The customer's legal team asks whether a fine-tuned model can leak one client's data to another. Answer mechanistically first, then tell me what you would change in the architecture and what you would be willing to commit to in the contract.
proofOfWork: Build a public repo, `lora-or-not`, that is a single reproducible bake-off rather than a notebook. It takes one real labelled dataset of roughly 1000 examples from a customer-like domain, splits it by entity (not by row) after MinHash deduplication, and runs four arms through one shared eval harness: (1) the prompted baseline with a pinned prompt hash and model snapshot, (2) few-shot plus strict output schema, (3) a QLoRA SFT of a 7B-class open-weights model, and (4) a cheap discriminative arm — embeddings plus logistic regression, or a fine-tuned encoder. `RESULTS.md` reports every arm on the same untouched test set with task metric, bootstrap 95% CI, McNemar p-value against the baseline, format-validity rate, p95 latency, and cost per 1000 calls, plus a break-even monthly volume where the tune's inference savings repay its build cost. Add three things that make it a senior artefact rather than a tutorial: an ablation sweeping `r` in {4, 8, 16, 64} and attention-only versus attention-plus-MLP `target_modules`, with the trainable-parameter count and eval delta for each; a catastrophic-forgetting holdout of 50 off-distribution tasks scored before and after tuning; and a `serving/` benchmark comparing `merge_and_unload()` against vLLM runtime adapters at 1, 4, and 16 concurrent distinct adapters. Finally commit a `FAILURES.md` where you deliberately reproduce two of this topic's classic bugs — a chat-template mismatch between training and serving, and a `target_modules` list that matches nothing — with the loss curves, `print_trainable_parameters()` output, and eval scores each one produces, so you can recognise them from the symptom alone in front of a customer. Ship a `MODEL_CARD.md` for the adapter with the pinned base revision, data provenance, eval numbers, and retraining trigger.
